implementation_notes: C++ is the idiom's home language, but it only supplies the pieces (virtual functions, covariant return types since C++98, `unique_ptr` since C++11) - the clone function itself is written by hand in every concrete class, so support is `manual`. Since C++11 the canonical modern form is `virtual std::unique_ptr<Shape> clone() const = 0;` overridden as `std::unique_ptr<Shape> clone() const override { return std::make_unique<Circle>(*this); }`: ownership is explicit and a container of `unique_ptr` becomes copyable again through clone(). Covariance does not extend to smart-pointer templates (`unique_ptr<Circle>` is unrelated to `unique_ptr<Shape>`), so overrides return the base pointer type; a separate covariant raw-pointer clone is the usual escape hatch for callers that already know the concrete type (C++ Core Guidelines C.130). For a closed type set, `std::variant` plus `std::visit` replaces the virtual hook with a checked, stack-friendly copy table.
pitfalls: Expecting covariance through smart pointers: `std::unique_ptr<Circle>` does not override `std::unique_ptr<Shape>`; keep the base return type or add a separate covariant raw-pointer helper.
Omitting the virtual destructor makes `delete base_ptr` on a cloned (or original) derived object undefined behaviour - the classic clone-without-virtual-dtor bug.

An intermediate abstract class that fails to re-declare `clone() = 0` lets a concrete class forget the override and silently inherit an implementation that returns the wrong dynamic type; slicing through a dereferenced clone (copying `*clone()` into a `Shape` value) has the same effect.

variants.name: Virtual clone with covariant raw pointer (C++98)
variants.idiom_name: `virtual Shape* clone() const` overridden as `Circle* clone() const`
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-C++11 form (and the form the More C++ Idioms write-up starts from): `virtual Shape* clone() const = 0;` overridden with a covariant return `Circle* clone() const { return new Circle(*this); }`. Covariant return types were standardised in C++98, so a caller that statically knows the concrete type gets it back without a downcast; the price is raw-pointer ownership - who deletes must be documented, and every early return or exception between the call and ownership is a leak. Choose it in C++98/03 codebases or where covariance is genuinely needed; the caller should adopt the pointer into an owning smart pointer immediately.
pitfalls: Raw-pointer returns leak on every path that does not reach the matching delete, including exceptions thrown while the pointer is still in flight.
Covariance applies only to pointer/reference return types - never to `unique_ptr`/`shared_ptr` wrappers - so the covariant form and the modern owning form must be kept in sync by hand.
Deleting the clone through the base pointer still requires a virtual destructor - covariance makes the return type precise, not the destruction polymorphic.

variants.name: CRTP clone mixin
variants.idiom_name: `template <class D> class Cloneable : public Shape` injecting `clone()`
variants.implementation_notes: A mixin writes the near-identical clone body once: `template <class D> class Cloneable : public Shape { std::unique_ptr<Shape> clone() const override { return std::make_unique<D>(static_cast<const D&>(*this)); } };`, so each concrete class only inherits `Cloneable<Circle>` and keeps its copy constructor. It trades covariance and explicit per-class control for less boilerplate, and it composes with the modern owning return. The static cast is safe only while `D` really is the most-derived type, and the mixin becomes part of the hierarchy that factories, serializers and `dynamic_cast`-style code must know about.
pitfalls: The mixin's `static_cast<const D&>` is undefined behaviour if `D` is not the most-derived type, so the mixin must not be combined carelessly with multiple or virtual inheritance.
A class that forgets to inherit `Cloneable<D>` (or inherits it with the wrong argument) keeps the pure/abstract `clone` or produces infinite recursion - a compile error only by luck.
Covariance is lost: `clone()` always returns the base pointer, so callers that know the concrete type must still downcast.
